children: The Pentagon is asking Congress to approve nearly $1.5 billion in funding transfers for artificial intelligence infrastructure, Textron’s MV-75 aircraft program and several operational priorities, Breaking Defense reported Wednesday, citing government documents.
The July request would redirect about $1.2 billion from fiscal 2026 accounts and $212 million from fiscal 2025 funding. Approval is required from congressional defense committees.

The largest proposed transfer is $600 million for a classified high-performance computing center. The facility would provide hardware and integration services needed to expand AI and machine-learning capabilities across the military’s secure intelligence network. Pentagon officials characterized the project as an urgent modernization priority.

For investors, the request signals continued growth in federal spending on AI computing, cybersecurity, military aviation and counter-drone systems. Potential beneficiaries include defense technology providers, data-center equipment suppliers and Textron, though the transfers still require congressional approval and could be modified or rejected.
The Army also wants to redirect $350 million to the MV-75 Cheyenne tiltrotor program, including $230 million from fiscal 2026 and $120 million from fiscal 2025. The funding would help Textron
build and test eight prototypes ahead of planned production in fiscal 2028.

The Pentagon warned that a funding shortfall could interrupt work, delay production and affect thousands of jobs across the aircraft’s supplier network. The additional money also would cover supplier cost increases and help complete the aircraft’s critical design review.

Other proposed transfers include $18 million to purchase six long-endurance Army drones and related equipment, partly for operations connected with the conflict involving Iran. Another $36 million would accelerate a tactical command system and counter-drone testing.
The Pentagon also seeks $40 million for supply-chain cybersecurity and acquisition oversight, along with another $40 million for a classified Special Operations Command program.

To help finance the changes, the department would remove $166 million from programs that train and equip partner forces fighting Islamic State militants in Iraq and Syria. The Pentagon said operational constraints and changes involving Syrian partner forces had reduced its ability to use that funding.

title: Pentagon seeks $1.5B funding shift for AI, Textron aircraft, drones
